Kirk’s own 1987 discussion, p. 4/n6, explicitly attributes this objection to Foster, with p. 43 locator; p. 47/n143 identifies Foster’s criticism of the idealist thrust. This confirms a particular materialist criticism without treating it as opposition to language study itself.

Confirmed in Kirk’s stated program and conclusion. He simultaneously endorses opposition to economic reductionism, contextual complexity and attention to language/politics. Not a simple rejection of linguistic investigation.

Bibliographic existence confirmed independently by Astra. This article’s particular argument, reply targets and differences from the 1987 critique remain unverified here; do not infer them from the title or transfer 1987 claims.

Confirmed in selected chapter 7 text. Wood expressly distinguishes Jones’s substantial historical work from other abstract theorists, and targets the conclusions drawn from his evidence. His rejection of mechanical correspondence need not entail general non-correspondence. A separate 1995 passage explains inherited radicalism’s transformation under capitalist relations.

The 1990 book’s existence and topic are confirmed, but its detailed treatment is not freshly read. A new arrow uses Palmer’s own independently read 1993 article, pp. 143–146, rather than silently substituting it as proof of the 1990 book’s exact claims.

Confirmed. Epstein praises the reinterpretation and the reality of language, then argues that ritual, collective solidarity and conflict over public terms cannot be reduced to formal ideology. He retains the importance of inherited traditions while making their meanings contested.
Book metadata confirmed by Astra. Its specific argument and relation to the 1986 essay remain unverified here; no assertion that it simply reprints that essay or repeats all its criticisms.

Kirk p. 5/n7 explicitly places Pickering among the critics whose general lines he follows in defending Chartism’s social/class character. Eley/Nield p. 7/n19 lists it among substantive contributions postdating Jones’s intervention and carrying discussion beyond his essay. These confirm a relevant response, but no detailed reconstruction of Pickering’s individual examples or conclusions is claimed from his title alone.

Kirk p. 4/n6 explicitly quotes Gray p. 367 on post-structuralist language analysis as a field of debate, and attributes the criticism of narrow formal words rather than constructed social meaning to Gray and Foster. This supports a bounded methodological objection, not blanket hostility to language.
